To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the ubiquitin ligase Highwire (Hiw) is a conserved negative regulator of axon guidance, (ii) Hiw is a negative regulator of the NMJ, (iii) Hiw regulates both axon guidance and NMJ by controlling ubiquitylation and turnover of a conserved set of proteins, and (iv) the molecular mechanisms underlying axon guidance and synapse function are surprisingly conserved.

the conserved PHR E3 ubiquitin-ligase regulates the stability of key regulators of NMJ and growth cone development, and that this function is required for proper NMJ formation and axon guidance during embryonic development.

PHR (Pam, highwire, Rpm-1), a conserved E3 ligase, regulates the activity and function of a ubiquitin proteasomal degradation pathway in both axonal targeting during development and NMJ formation and function in the adult.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of axonal targeting and synaptic development in the Drosophila neuromuscular system.
the identification and characterization of genes and molecular pathways that control axonal targeting, synaptic development and plasticity.
how the nervous system is built and how it works, and we use the Drosophila model organism to study these questions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the highwire pathway is essential for both embryonic and adult synaptic function.
the PHR pathway is essential for the development and function of synapses and growth cones.
PHR regulates the degradation of specific proteins that are essential for both axonal growth cone guidance and for the formation and function of synapses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PHR controls a protein degradation pathway that regulates both the formation and function of synapses.

PHR is a master regulator that controls a common degradation pathway that is used to target proteins to different cellular locations, such as the synapse and growth cone, during different stages of neuronal development.
PHR is a master regulator of the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) that controls the formation and function of synapses and growth cones.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the molecular machinery controlling the formation and function of NMJ and axonal targeting during development are surprisingly similar, suggesting the possibility that the same molecular pathways are involved in both processes.
the same molecular pathway controls the function and formation of synapses and growth cones on two sides of PHR.
the PHR pathway is essential for both the embryonic and adult nervous system, and that the same pathway controls distinct aspects of neuronal development and function in these two stages of life.
